title: Oriented Intersection Theory
notes: Open by naming the upgrade from mod two counting to signed counting. The lecture treats orientation as a bookkeeping device that turns local tangent data into integers, then follows those integers through intersections, fixed points, vector fields, degree, and Euler characteristic.

title: The Sign Pipeline
notes: Use this route slide to give students a single mental model for a long chapter. Each construction asks for a local sign, sums the signs, and then proves that the resulting integer is stable under the allowed geometric motion.

title: Orientation Is A Determinant Choice
notes: Emphasize that orientation is not an arrow drawn on the whole space. It is an equivalence class of ordered bases, and a chart is compatible with the orientation only when the relevant transition determinant preserves that sign.

title: Oriented Manifolds Need Compatible Charts
notes: Make the atlas condition concrete. A single chart can declare positive coordinates locally, but an oriented manifold requires these declarations to agree on overlaps. The determinant of every transition Jacobian is the local test that prevents sign contradictions.

title: A Transverse Crossing Has A Local Sign
notes: Pause on the order of tangent spaces. At a complementary-dimensional transverse intersection, concatenate a positive basis for one submanifold with a positive basis for the other, compare it with the ambient orientation, and record plus one or minus one.

title: Algebraic Counts Can Cancel
notes: Use the two-crossing example to explain why signed counting is stronger than bare counting. Two geometric intersection points may contribute opposite local signs, so the algebraic intersection number can vanish even while the visible crossings remain.

title: Homotopy Moves Crossings In Pairs
notes: The invariance story is a local movie. Under a generic deformation, crossings trace one-dimensional tracks, and births or deaths occur as opposite-sign pairs. That is why the signed sum is stable even though individual intersection points move.

title: Fixed Points Are Intersections
notes: Translate fixed point theory into the intersection language. A fixed point of a map is exactly a point where the graph meets the diagonal, and transversality of that intersection is controlled by the invertibility of I minus the derivative.

title: Circle Maps Reveal The Lefschetz Count
notes: Use the circle model as a transparent check on signs. For the degree d map on the circle, the Lefschetz number is one minus d, and simple transverse fixed points contribute the sign suggested by the linear factor one minus d.

title: Vector-Field Index Is A Winding Number
notes: Draw attention to the normalized vector field on a small circle around an isolated zero. The local index is the degree of this circle-to-circle map, so sources, saddles, and rotations can be compared by how their arrows wind.

title: Poincare-Hopf Sums The Local Indices
notes: Frame Poincare-Hopf as the vector-field analogue of oriented intersection counting. Each zero contributes an integer index, and on a compact oriented manifold the total cannot be chosen freely; it must equal the Euler characteristic. Stress that this makes vector fields remember topology, even when the arrows are drawn locally.

title: Hopf Degree Is The Global Version Of Local Sign
notes: Present degree as the same mechanism after replacing one crossing by a whole fiber over a regular value. A smooth map between oriented manifolds of the same dimension assigns signs to inverse images, and Hopf's theorem makes the resulting integer homotopy invariant.

title: Euler Characteristic Has Many Costumes
notes: Connect the chapter's differential and combinatorial languages. Euler characteristic can be computed from cells, predicted by a vector field through Poincare-Hopf, and constrained by degree and fixed point information in related settings. The point is that different calculations are checking the same integer.

title: One Sign Engine Drives Several Theorems
notes: Use the dependency map to keep the chapter from feeling like disconnected named results. Orientation provides local signs, local signs build integer invariants, and the theorems explain which geometric problems those integers can solve. Encourage students to trace any theorem back to its sign source.

title: Sign Diagnostics For Computations
notes: This slide turns the theory into a practical checklist for the notebook. Every computation should state the determinant, degree, or winding number that supplies its sign, then compare the local contributions with the expected global invariant.

title: What The Chapter Leaves Behind
notes: Close by returning to the main habit of thought. Oriented intersection theory teaches students to replace fragile pictures by signed local data, then trust the integer only after checking transversality, orientation conventions, and deformation invariance.
